question: What is "credential stuffing"?

options.text: Creating an extremely long, complex password
Automatically trying stolen username/password pairs from one breach against many other websites
Guessing a password one character at a time
A type of two-factor authentication

explanation: Attackers take huge lists of leaked username/password pairs from one breached site and automatically try the same combinations on other unrelated sites, betting that people reuse passwords.

question: Why is reusing the same password across multiple accounts risky, even if the password itself is strong?

options.text: It's not actually risky if the password is strong enough
If any one site is breached, that same password can be tried automatically against your other accounts
Websites are technically unable to store passwords
Strong passwords can't be reused by definition

explanation: Strength only protects against guessing — it does nothing if the exact password leaks from a breach elsewhere and gets tried against your other accounts directly.

question: According to industry breach data, what's the single most common way attackers first get into an account or system?

options.text: Guessing random passwords one at a time
Using stolen or reused credentials
Physically stealing a device
Exploiting a network printer

explanation: Credential abuse is consistently reported as the single leading initial attack vector in breach investigations — ahead of exploited software vulnerabilities and phishing.

question: What's the most effective way to prevent one breached password from compromising your other accounts?

options.text: Use a unique password for every account, ideally with a password manager
Change your password every single day
Use the same very long password everywhere
Write all your passwords on paper in one place

explanation: A unique password per account means a breach at one site simply can't be reused anywhere else — a password manager makes this practical without having to memorize dozens of passwords.

question: If you get a notification that a service you use was breached, what should you do?

options.text: Ignore it if you didn't personally receive an email about it
Change your password on that service, and on any other account where you reused the same password
Delete your account there permanently
Wait to see if anything bad actually happens first

explanation: The breached password should be treated as compromised everywhere it was reused, not just on the one site that was actually breached.
